established_findings.statement: LLMs show promise for NetOps tasks (intent translation, config synthesis, RCA), but operational reliability largely depends on surrounding tooling, validators, and workflow machinery rather than on the model alone.
limitations: Evidence is primarily survey/position and prototype-reporting; not all claims validated at Internet-scale production.
Degree of dependence on external tooling varies by task and deployment.

established_findings.statement: Agentic LLM systems exhibit a broad, documented set of failure modes (reasoning/planning errors, tool/action execution errors, memory/context problems, coordination failures); formal taxonomies and evaluation protocols have been proposed.
limitations: Taxonomies synthesize published reports but do not quantify prevalence across all NetOps deployments.
Practical mitigation effectiveness depends on system implementation.

established_findings.statement: Closed-loop generate→validate→repair pipelines (including simulation/NDT, retrieval/validation, and iterative revision) improve end-to-end execution success in configuration/deployment and playbook/execution tasks relative to naive generation.
limitations: Improvements are task- and dataset-specific; reported gains differ across studies.
Not all domains (vendor CLIs, production WANs) have comparable published evaluation suites.

established_findings.statement: Deterministic/formal network-verification tools and domain-specific verification systems (NetKAT/Weighted NetKAT, Hoyan, MEV, VeriFlow-style approaches) are effective for checking reachability, isolation, and change-impact properties and have been scaled and deployed in production contexts.
limitations: Verification requires an accurate formal model/translation of network artifacts; creating and maintaining such models can be costly.
Verifiers cover specific property classes; they do not eliminate upstream translation errors.

established_findings.statement: Constrained-generation approaches (schema-guided generation, DSLs, schema-preserving repair) substantially reduce structural and schema errors in generated configuration-like artifacts.
limitations: Schema/syntax validity does not guarantee semantic correctness (reachability, policy compliance).
Constrained methods may require additional engineering (schemas, DSLs, validators) per vendor/task.

established_findings.statement: Reasoning-augmentation techniques such as chain-of-thought (CoT) and retrieval-augmentation (RAG) can improve LLM outputs in some NetOps-related reasoning tasks, but they are not universally beneficial and can degrade structured/numerical accuracy in some settings.
limitations: Effects are task-dependent; some studies report strong gains while others report degradation for numerical/structured outputs.
Proper grounding and deterministic post-checks influence net benefit.

unresolved_questions.statement: To what extent do LLM-agent NetOps pipelines generalize across heterogeneous, production-scale networks (multi-vendor, large-scale topologies) without human-in-the-loop gating?
limitations: Existing production reports and benchmarks are encouraging but limited in breadth and independent replication.
Published field trials often include human oversight or constrained scopes.

unresolved_questions.statement: Which architectural pattern is generally superior for safe NetOps automation: (A) LLM→formal-model translation + solver (translation-first) or (B) end-to-end agentic LLMs with integrated validators and rollback (agentic-first)?
limitations: Existing work argues for both approaches but lacks head-to-head, multi-task comparisons under shared evaluation metrics.
Task characteristics likely determine the preferred architecture.

unresolved_questions.statement: What are robust, task-general best practices (prompts, decoding settings, validator integration) that minimize semantic hallucinations across vendor-specific network configuration generation?
limitations: Available studies show mixed results; many evaluate limited model families, vendors, or tasks.
Decoding/prompt effects interact with model size, fine-tuning, and retrieval.

candidate_gaps.statement: A systematic empirical comparison is lacking that measures end-to-end operational correctness (reachability, isolation, policy compliance, safe rollback) of (i) constrained-DSL + deterministic verifier pipelines vs (ii) generate→validate→repair agentic pipelines across multiple vendor CLIs and realistic topologies.
limitations: Literature contains components of such comparisons but not a unified, multi-vendor, multi-metric study.
Building such a benchmark requires curated vendor datasets and verified simulators/emulators.

candidate_gaps.statement: There is a need for standardized, workflow-centered NetOps benchmarks that report operational metrics (execution success, reachability correctness, rollback safety, false positive/negative of validators) for LLM-driven agents; existing benchmarks (e.g., ITBench) show low agent success but do not yet cover full NetOps property suites.
limitations: ITBench and related efforts provide initial scenarios but are limited in scope and task diversity.
Standardization requires community agreement on properties and acceptance criteria.

candidate_gaps.statement: Reliable, LLM-assisted translation pipelines that produce formally checkable models (automated, verifiable translation of live configs/topology into NetKAT/NetModel) need more validation and tooling to be practical at scale.
limitations: TypoNet and NetKAT work are promising but require more cross-vendor evaluation and robustness testing.
Translation correctness is a single-point dependency for downstream verification.

excluded_claims: LLMs are ready to perform fully autonomous, unsupervised production NetOps change execution without validators, human approval, or rollback mechanisms (unsupported by supplied records).
Chain-of-thought prompting universally and reliably eliminates hallucinations in configuration generation (evidence shows task-dependent effects and possible degradation).
Deterministic verification tools are unnecessary if an LLM is sufficiently capable (contradicted by surveys and deployment reports emphasizing surrounding machinery).
A single LLM model family has been shown to generalize across all NetOps vendors and tasks without per-vendor adaptation or verification (no supplied record supports this broad claim).
